meaning.evidence: Every beat survives in order: the girls' relief, the every-year joke, Tater as "the Vice Turkey", the clemency ("to let 'em off the hook this arvo"), the economic list, the creed, "Yes, We Cran" and the leftovers closer. Nothing is invented.

sense.evidence: Most terms fit: "stoked" for the girls' relief, "aviator sunnies", "tip me hat", "every man and his dog has a feed". "the crook and the oldies" uses "crook" (sick) as a noun for sick people, which strains, and "the battlers" narrows "the poor" a little.

authenticity.evidence: Natural drawl throughout ("'Course, we've got heaps to be thankful", "Ya don't reckon that's funny?", "some shockers in here"). A few joins wobble: "me last presidential turkey pardon" next to "my great privilege", and "we're rapt to be joined" is a slightly formal frame for rapt.

register.evidence: Consistent g-dropping and a steady sprinkle of slang ("arvo", "sunnies", "heaps", "some bugger at yer table"), but it stays close to the original's sentences; more a level-4 retelling than a full pub yarn. Swearing is light and within the dial.

tone.evidence: The jokes land as jokes ("No way I'm givin' this habit up cold turkey", "Yes, We Cran") and the earnest middle stays earnest ("out of many, we are one").

flow.evidence: Reads cleanly aloud; "We're workin' on gettin' him a pair of aviator sunnies" and the closer run smoothly. Uniform apostrophe-dropping ("Thanksgivin'" every time) gets a little mechanical.

variety.evidence: "heaps" carries a lot of weight ("we've got heaps to be thankful", "there's heaps of families", "We've got heaps more in common"), and the -in' drop is applied to almost every word.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the pardon speech: the puns, the self-deprecating "let's just say it's me job", the patriotic turn, all intact.

problems.quote: the crook and the oldies
problems.original: the sick and the elderly
problems.why: "crook" is an adjective; "the crook" as a noun for sick people reads awkwardly and could suggest criminals.

problems.quote: we've got heaps to be thankful for
problems.original: we have a lot to be thankful for
problems.why: "heaps" is leaned on across the speech.

problems.quote: this is me last presidential turkey pardon
problems.original: this is my final presidential turkey pardon
problems.why: "me" for "my" is used inconsistently alongside "my great privilege", so it reads as applied rather than voiced.

A.summary: A faithful, natural level-4 retelling that keeps every joke and the earnest middle; a touch light for level 5 and leans on "heaps".

meaning.evidence: All points kept: "Tater's only here on the bench", "to let 'em off the hook this arvo", the full economic list ("The stock market's near enough tripled"), "Yes, We Cran" and the leftovers line. Small rewordings ("hopes they'll have it better") keep the sense.

sense.evidence: "on the bench" fits the backup role exactly, "the haves and have-nots" fits inequality, "We're a mob that looks out for each other" fits. "the crook and the oldies" again strains as a noun.

authenticity.evidence: Sounds spoken: "Beaut one, that. Pretty funny.", "Not funny, ya reckon?", "near enough tripled". Idiom sits where an Australian would put it.

register.evidence: More reworked than a light pass ("finally swap the polls for the poultry", "after a long old campaign season") but still follows the speech sentence by sentence; just short of a full level-5 yarn. Swearing ("some bugger at yer table") within the dial.

tone.evidence: Comic timing preserved ("Aw, it's not that bad. Come on, now.") and the solemn passages stay sincere ("Acceptin' our differences and buildin' a diverse society has never been easy, but it's never mattered more").

flow.evidence: Smooth throughout; rephrasings like "what binds us isn't any one race or religion, it's stickin' to a common creed" read as if written that way.

variety.evidence: Wider spread than A ("on the bench", "haves and have-nots", "mob", "near enough"), though "heaps" still recurs ("there's heaps of families", "There's heaps more we've got in common").

essence.evidence: The speech's shape, puns and patriotic turn all survive: "Now that's worth gobblin' about."

problems.quote: the crook and the oldies
problems.original: the sick and the elderly
problems.why: "crook" as a noun for sick people is strained.

problems.quote: There's heaps more we've got in common than what divides us.
problems.original: We have a lot more in common than divides us.
problems.why: "heaps" repeated several times across the text.

B.summary: Polished, natural and faithful, with the jokes and the earnest middle intact; slightly lighter than a full level-5 yarn.

meaning.evidence: Every point is there, with colour hung off it ("Over the moon, the pair of 'em", "in case Tot pulls a hammy", "Got the job, never gets a run"). One addition goes past colour into a new claim: "not to be one bad day from a hospital bill they can't pay"; and "hopes they'll have it better than we did" adds a comparison.

sense.evidence: "pulls a hammy" and "never gets a run" fit the backup-player joke; "longer than a wet week" fits the long campaign; "doin' it tough" fits those needing a hand. "the crook and the oldies" still strains.

authenticity.evidence: Reads like a real Aussie speaker: "a campaign season that went on longer than a wet week", "never been a walk in the park", "Gold, that.", "Yeah, yeah, I heard it."

register.evidence: A full pub-yarn retelling with asides throughout ("Pretty funny, if I say so meself", "rollin' up the sleeves"), and swearing at the light end of the dial ("how bloody lucky we are", "some bugger at yer table"). That is the weight a level-5 brief asks for.

tone.evidence: Adds jokes in the same spirit ("Aw, it's not that bad, little fella") while keeping the solemn passages sincere ("we've gotta keep fightin' discrimination in all its forms").

flow.evidence: Mostly smooth, but some added clauses lengthen sentences: "who finally know what it's like not to be one bad day from a hospital bill they can't pay, cos they've got health insurance" is a mouthful.

variety.evidence: Wide range of fresh idiom ("wet week", "pulls a hammy", "walk in the park", "dead set on this", "Gold, that") with little leaning.

essence.evidence: Still the farewell pardon speech, puns and all, with the asides reacting to its own jokes ("Got the job, never gets a run").

problems.quote: not to be one bad day from a hospital bill they can't pay
problems.original: who finally know the security of health insurance
problems.why: Adds a new claim about medical bills rather than colour on the original line.

problems.quote: hopes they'll have it better than we did
problems.original: we all have hopes for their better future
problems.why: Adds a comparison with the speaker's generation not in the original.

problems.quote: the crook and the oldies
problems.original: the sick and the elderly
problems.why: "crook" as a noun strains.

C.summary: The fullest and most natural yarn, right on the level-5 brief with jokes that suit the speech; a couple of additions edge into new claims.

meaning.evidence: All points survive. "just in case Tot can't pull his weight on the day" shifts "can't fulfill his duties" towards slacking, and "That was a ripper, that one" replaces "That was pretty funny" but keeps the self-congratulation.

sense.evidence: Most terms fit ("aviator sunnies", "a generous, giving sort of country", "health cover"). "pull his weight" implies laziness rather than unavailability, and "the crook and the elderly" strains.

authenticity.evidence: Some natural lines ("Come on now, mate.", "never been a walk in the park"), but "a long arse of a campaign season" is an awkward form (Australians say a long-arse campaign), and "the number of folks without health cover" uses US "folks".

register.evidence: Keeps standard spelling and much of the original wording ("Wages are going up again. Inequality's narrowing."); swears are within the dial ("Every bloody year", "long arse"). Noticeably lighter than a level-5 pub yarn.

tone.evidence: Jokes kept, solemn passages kept, but "after a long arse of a campaign season" jars in a line about gathering with loved ones and blessings.

flow.evidence: Reads easily for the most part; "a long arse of a campaign season" and the double "I reckon we're judged... I reckon that to really live up" are clunky.

variety.evidence: Slang is thin and repeats ("I reckon" twice running, "'em"), with long stretches of plain English: "Our high school graduation rate's at an all-time high."

essence.evidence: Recognisably the speech throughout, every pun intact: "Yes, We Cran."

problems.quote: after a long arse of a campaign season
problems.original: after a long campaign season
problems.why: Unidiomatic form of long-arse, and an Australian would wince at it in the blessings line.

problems.quote: the number of folks without health cover
problems.original: our uninsured rate
problems.why: "folks" is American.

problems.quote: can't pull his weight on the day
problems.original: can't fulfill his duties
problems.why: "pull his weight" implies slacking, not being unable to serve.

problems.quote: I reckon that to really live up to those ideals
problems.original: I believe that in order to truly live up to those ideals
problems.why: Repeats "I reckon" from the sentence before.

D.summary: Faithful but light for level 5, with one awkward swear and thin, repeated slang.

meaning.evidence: Several lines change sense: "the brave turkeys who weren't lucky as fuck" garbles "weren't so lucky", "proved that they weren't chook" kills the chicken/coward pun, "Yep, We Cran" breaks the "Yes, We Can" pun, and "no matter what some drongo reckons" adds a claim. "Anyway, every year." breaks the joke's build.

sense.evidence: Many terms take the wrong sense: "weren't lucky as fuck", "weren't chook", "millions of little buggers" for children, "every bastard who's tryin' to get a second chance" for refugees and immigrants.

authenticity.evidence: Stock interjections bolted onto sentence starts ("Jeez Louise, Malia and Sasha", "Crikey, so he's sort of like the Vice Turkey", "Struth, and it's my bloody great privilege", "Well, Inequality is narrowing") with the original's prose left in between.

register.evidence: Most sentences are the original word for word ("The housing market is healing. The stock market has nearly tripled.") with tags on top; swearing stays within the dial but is sprayed ("Oh, shit, and there are many families of servicemembers"). Not a level-5 retelling.

tone.evidence: The sincere passages are undercut: "Oh, shit, and there are many families of servicemembers who had empty chairs at the table" makes a sombre line flippant, and "every bastard" for the vulnerable sounds contemptuous.

flow.evidence: Jarring joins everywhere: "Mate, low unemployment. Wages are rising again. Well, Inequality is narrowing.", "values'n ideals", and the typo "come one" kept.

variety.evidence: The same tags recur: "Mate," "Anyway," "bloody" ("me bloody privilege", "yer bloody table", "Bloody hell").

essence.evidence: The skeleton of the speech is there, but its signature puns are broken ("weren't chook", "Yep, We Cran") and the warmth is gone.

problems.quote: the brave turkeys who weren't lucky as fuck
problems.original: the brave turkeys who weren't so lucky
problems.why: Garbles the meaning; reads as if the turkeys were extremely unlucky or lucky, and is crude in the mock-solemn line.

problems.quote: proved that they weren't chook
problems.original: proved that they weren't chicken
problems.why: "chicken" means cowardly; "chook" loses the pun and the sense.

problems.quote: Yep, We Cran
problems.original: Yes, We Cran
problems.why: Breaks the pun on the "Yes, We Can" slogan, the punchline.

problems.quote: Oh, shit, and there are many families of servicemembers
problems.original: And there are many families of servicemembers
problems.why: Swear tacked onto the most sombre line inverts its tone.

problems.quote: every bastard who's tryin' to get a second chance
problems.original: everybody who's trying to get a second chance
problems.why: Sounds contemptuous of the vulnerable people the line is about.

problems.quote: millions of little buggers
problems.original: including millions of children
problems.why: Wrong register for children covered by health insurance.

problems.quote: no matter what some drongo reckons
problems.why: Adds a jab not in the original.

problems.quote: Jeez Louise, Malia and Sasha
problems.original: Malia and Sasha, by the way
problems.why: Stock interjections bolted onto sentence starts throughout; stage-Australian.

problems.quote: Anyway, every year.
problems.original: Every year.
problems.why: "Anyway" deflates the deadpan repetition the joke depends on.

E.summary: Mostly untranslated with interjections and swears bolted on; breaks the key puns and makes the solemn passages flippant.
